subject: ent
title: Vocal cord paralysis

steps.tx: The **recurrent laryngeal nerve** supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid (external superior laryngeal nerve), with asymmetric course: right loops subclavian artery, left loops aortic arch through thorax, making left palsy commoner from lung, aortic and mediastinal disease. Vagus lesions high add palate and pharynx signs; superior laryngeal injury (thyroid surgery) loses pitch range and projection (singers) via cricothyroid tension failure and supraglottic sensation (internal branch) aspiration.
steps.say: Left cord nerve tours chest, so left palsies hunt lungs. Pitch loss after thyroid surgery is superior nerve, not recurrent.

steps.tx: **Key point.** Causes by segment: skull base and jugular foramen syndromes, neck surgery (thyroid, carotid, cervical spine anterior approach), malignancy (lung apex Pancoast, thyroid, oesophagus), aortic aneurysm (Ortner cardiovocal syndrome: left palsy from enlarged left atrium or aorta), intubation trauma (arytenoid dislocation mimics palsy but is mechanical), viral idiopathic (post viral neuritis pattern) and central strokes. Any unexplained palsy images nerve course from skull base to aortopulmonary window (CT contrast).
steps.say: No cause given for palsy: scan from skull base to chest window. Big heart can silence left cord (Ortner).

steps.tx: **Key point.** Examination: flexible laryngoscopy shows paramedian or lateral (cadaveric in high vagal) cord position, bowing, pooled secretions and aspiration; stroboscopy grades vibration for voice work. Unilateral palsy voices breathy, diplophonic, fatigues, coughs weakly and aspirates thin fluids. Management: speech therapy first, early temporary injection medialisation (months resorbing gels) when aspiration or professional voice demands, permanent medialisation thyroplasty or arytenoid adduction after recovery window (about 9 to 12 months for neurapraxia), reinnervation in selected young patients.
steps.say: Inject early for swallow safety, frame surgery after a year if nerve stays dead.

steps.tx: **Bilateral palsy** is airway disease: cords rest near midline (recurrent nerves, abductor posterior cricoarytenoid only opener fails) causing inspiratory stridor with surprisingly preserved voice, after thyroid surgery, malignancy or neurological disease. Tracheostomy secures severe obstruction; later cordotomy, arytenoidectomy or lateralisation trades voice quality for airway. Bilateral paralysis with stridor must never be sedated or scoped casually without airway plan.
steps.say: Two midline cords whisper well but breathe badly. Airway surgery buys breath with voice currency.
